## Task
Generate the central ascii tree diagram for the layout

## Layout
This section will contain details on the high-level layout of the data
For now, we will use a single layout to display the data
This layout uses a single central ascii tree diagram and then some diagrams on the side

## General
I want you to use CanvasView to create a view that explains this current feature. The following are some guidelines:
- relations
  - edges
    - obvious -> just the edge
    - less obvious -> edge + edge text
      > "inherits", "imports", "MCP API call", etc..
    - less less obvious
      > creating an "anchor" node / tree at the source or target or both
- tree-diagrams
  - tree are best to depict nested, hierarchals arrangements of the data
    > their strength lies in their ability to segment non-adjacent levels of the data-space
  - while uniformity / flat levels are good, I suspect this is not always the case and not always the best use of trees
- highlighting
  - can be used to mark nodes as important

generation.prompt:
Draw one ASCII tree over this source code, using only plain ASCII (+--, |, `--)
and naming only code objects: types, fields, functions, values. No files or
folders.

Let ownership be the trunk: each object branches into the data it is
responsible for. Beneath any object, grow up to three small limbs when they
apply: "owns", "called by", and "needs". Everything lives inside the tree as
a branch or leaf, with nothing written off to the side.

"needs" limbs reach toward other parts of the tree. Rather than regrowing
what they point at, end them in a leaf that names the object, so the tree
stays a tree while still showing where it is tied to itself.

Illustrative shape (use actual code object names from the supplied source):
```
CanvasViews
+-- SavedView
|   +-- owns
|   |   +-- checkpointIds
|   |   +-- finalCheckpointId
|   |   `-- forkCheckpointId
|   +-- called by
|   |   +-- create()
|   |   `-- fork()
|   `-- needs
|       `-- Checkpoint
`-- Session
    +-- owns
    |   +-- activeViewId
    |   `-- workingCopies
    `-- called by
        +-- open()
        `-- save()
```

Draw one ASCII tree over this source code, plain ASCII only, naming only code
objects. No files or folders.

Let depth carry the meaning, so the shape alone explains the code. At the top
are the types. Beneath each type, the data it owns. Beneath each piece of
data, the functions that create, change, or retire it, as siblings in the
order they run. Beneath each function, the things it needs in order to do its
work, as leaves.

Every line's meaning should come from how deep it sits. Do not add labels to
explain it; let the branching do the explaining.

Illustrative shape (use actual code object names from the supplied source):
```
Session
+-- workingCopies
|   +-- open()
|   |   +-- activeViewId
|   |   `-- current canvas
|   `-- save()
|       `-- activeViewId
`-- activeViewId
    +-- create()
    |   `-- SavedView
    `-- discard()
        `-- parentViewId
```

generation.prompt:
Draw one ASCII tree over this source code, plain ASCII only, naming only code
objects. No files or folders.

Root the tree at what the program ultimately produces. Each branch beneath a
node is something that node needs in order to exist: data it is computed
from, the function that computes it, and the object that holds it. Let these
appear as their own branches, so who owns and who calls is woven into the
same shape as what needs what.

Leaves are where things start: user commands and stored data. When two
branches need the same object, grow it fully once, and elsewhere let it
appear as a bare leaf with just its name.

Illustrative shape (use actual code object names from the supplied source):
```
canvas after reopen
+-- resumeOrRestore()
|   +-- workingCopies[target]
|   |   +-- Session
|   |   `-- stash()
|   |       `-- current canvas
|   `-- finalCheckpointId
|       +-- SavedView
|       `-- save()
|           `-- Checkpoint
`-- Checkpoint
```

generation.prompt:
Keep the following in mind when generating your diagram:
- there should be 20/80 between code refs and nat lang
- you should use the hierarchal nature of the tree structure well
  - [BIAS] you have a tendency for using uniform data displays
  - this is sometimes good but it does not utilize the strength of trees as reprsentations, which allows meaning to be encoded in depth so when all layers are roughly same level, we lose the ability to easily spot the difference in segmenting the data
  - nested context also imparts meaning visually because children nodes will be interpreted in light of their parents
- try to represent the following in your graphs:
  Data relations
  Call (dynamic) which activation invoked which
  Ownership who is responsible for which storage

  Data dependency is a different kind of thing. It isn’t a fifth organizational choice; it is the record of what actually needs what for the program to compute its result. It’s a graph, and it exists before you decide how to organize anything.
